```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                     fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5)
old_seed <- if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE))
  get(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv) else NULL
library(imfeatures)
```

An image can contain very different kinds of structure in different places.
Think of regular stripes on one side and a patch of visual noise on the other.
A measurement of the whole image combines information from both regions. What
if you want the measurement to give more importance to one region?

A **saliency map** supplies a weight for each location in the image. It is often
shown as a heat map: brighter locations receive more weight. The values might
come from a model that predicts where people will look, or from a region you
have chosen to study. Here we will construct a simple map ourselves, so we know
exactly which part of the image it emphasizes.

The package uses **entropy** to summarize how spread out a distribution is.
For edge orientations, low entropy means that a few orientations account for
most of the edge strength; higher entropy means that strength is spread more
evenly across orientations. Regular stripes and visual noise therefore provide
a useful first example.

`compute_saliency_features()` returns three kinds of measurements:

- **First-order edge entropy:** how varied are the edge orientations in the
  regions receiving weight? This pools orientations across locations.
- **Pairwise (second-order) edge entropy:** how varied are the orientation
  relationships between edges at particular distances and directions from one
  another? This also takes their spatial arrangement into account.
- **Location entropy:** how concentrated is the heat map itself? A small bright
  spot concentrates weight in a small area; a broadly spread map distributes it
  over more of the image.

The distinction matters because the same bright spot can fall on either stripes
or noise. Moving that spot preserves the map's concentration but changes which
image features receive weight. We will use this idea to interpret the results.

## Build an example we can recognize by eye

We will put vertical stripes on the left and random noise on the right, then
place the heat map's bright spot over the stripes. Later, we will flip the map
so that it emphasizes the noise. We expect the stripes to have lower
first-order edge entropy because their edges occupy fewer orientations.

The code below creates two matrices: `img` holds the image values and `saliency`
holds the weights. Each weight belongs to the pixel at the same position in
`img`.

```{r image-and-map}
set.seed(104)
img <- outer(1:72, 1:80, function(x, y) sin(x * .6))
img[37:72, ] <- matrix(rnorm(36 * 80), 36, 80)
saliency <- outer(1:72, 1:80, function(x, y)
  exp(-((x - 21)^2 + (y - 45)^2) / 180))
```

```{r show-input, echo=FALSE}
(function() {
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1))
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  image(img, col = gray.colors(128), axes = FALSE, main = "Image")
  image(saliency, col = hcl.colors(128, "Inferno"), axes = FALSE, main = "Saliency weights")
})()
```

In the figure, brighter colors in the heat map mean that those parts of the
image will contribute more to the weighted edge measurements. For your own
data, check that the image and map have the same dimensions and orientation,
and cover the same area. A bright spot should sit over the feature you intend
to emphasize. With imager's matrix convention, the first dimension runs
horizontally. If you supply an image file, supply a map on that file's original
pixel grid; the function will resize them together if needed.

## Measure the image with and without the heat map

The function first detects edges in the image, then uses the map to weight
their contribution. Start by comparing three rows in its output:

- `observed` uses the map we supplied, with its bright spot over the stripes.
- `unweighted` gives every location the same saliency weight. Stronger image
  edges still contribute more than weaker ones.
- `flip_axis1` flips the supplied map horizontally, moving the bright spot
  onto the noise while leaving the image unchanged.

The function also returns other comparison maps, which we will explain below.
We use smaller filters and distance ranges to suit this small example. The
`ranges` entries specify inclusive histogram indices: index 1 represents
rounded distance zero, so indices 5 through 20 represent rounded distances
4 through 19 pixels. Keep pixel scale and viewing geometry consistent when
comparing different images.

```{r measure}
settings <- list(filter_length = 9L, gabor_bins = 8L, circ_bins = 16L,
                 maxdiag = 100L,
                 ranges = list(c(5L, 20L), c(21L, 40L), c(41L, 70L)))
elapsed <- system.time(
  result <- do.call(compute_saliency_features, c(
    list(image = img, saliency = saliency, representation = "weights",
         centre_match = TRUE, scales = c(1/16, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2)), settings))
)[["elapsed"]]
result$features[
  result$features$control %in% c("observed", "unweighted", "flip_axis1"),
  c("control", "first_order", "effective_fraction")
]
```

```{r validate-example, include=FALSE}
f <- result$features
stopifnot(is.finite(f$first_order[1]),
          f$first_order[1] < f$first_order[f$control == "flip_axis1"],
          result$metadata$counting_groups == 1L,
          isTRUE(all.equal(f$effective_fraction[1],
            f$effective_fraction[f$control == "centre_bias_matched"], tolerance = 1e-8)))
```

With the heat map over the stripes, first-order entropy is
`r round(f$first_order[1], 3)` bits. Flipping the map onto the noise raises it to
`r round(f$first_order[f$control == "flip_axis1"], 3)` bits. The measurement is
responding to the part of the image we emphasized, as intended. Because we made
this map ourselves, this example tells us about the weighting calculation; it
does not tell us where a person would actually look.

The `effective_fraction` column describes the map's concentration on a scale
from a single pixel's fraction of the image up to 1. A uniform map has a value
of 1. Our map has a value of `r round(f$effective_fraction[1], 3)`: it has the
same location entropy as distributing weight equally over approximately
`r round(100 * f$effective_fraction[1])`% of the image. This is a summary of the
whole weight distribution, rather than an area obtained by drawing a boundary
around the bright spot. Flipping the map preserves this value.

## Choose the representation and selection rule

Use `representation = "weights"` for nonnegative maps and `"log_density"` for
natural-log density outputs. Log values can be negative; `-Inf` means zero mass.
The package exponentiates stably and normalizes the map. Multiplying raw weights
by a positive constant, or adding a constant to log densities, leaves results
unchanged.

```{r representations}
raw_location <- saliency_location_entropy(saliency, "weights")
log_location <- saliency_location_entropy(log(saliency) - 1000, "log_density")
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(raw_location, log_location, tolerance = 1e-10)))
raw_location
```

Signed raw maps are rejected by default. `signed_policy = "rectify"` replaces
negative weights with zero; `"shift"` subtracts a negative minimum. Choose and
record a policy appropriate to the model: these choices change its map, and
neither turns arbitrary model scores into calibrated fixation probabilities.
Zero-mass maps return NA with a status, rather than a uniform fallback.

```{r signed-map}
saliency_location_entropy(matrix(c(-1, 0, 1, 2), 2), "weights",
                          signed_policy = "rectify")
```

The edge filters assign each location a strength, called its **response**, and
an orientation. First-order entropy uses all positive responses. Pairwise
entropy uses a subset of edges to keep computation manageable. The default
`edge_selection = "image"` selects them by response strength, then uses exactly
those edges for every comparison map. This
isolates reweighting. The legacy selection threshold retains the strongest
10,000 responses on larger images, including cutoff ties; below 10,000 pixels it
uses the strongest 10% instead. It is not an exact cap when responses tie.

`edge_selection = "saliency"` selects by response times saliency, so low-contrast
salient edges can enter. It measures the combined effect of selection and
weighting and may require separate counting passes for different controls.

```{r selection-sensitivity}
sensitivity <- do.call(compute_saliency_features, c(
  list(image = img, saliency = saliency, representation = "weights",
       edge_selection = "saliency", pair_weighting = "reference",
       transform_controls = FALSE), settings))
selected <- sensitivity$selection[c("observed", "unweighted")]
data.frame(control = names(selected),
           selected_edges = vapply(selected, nrow, integer(1)))
```

The default `pair_weighting = "both"` weights both endpoints of each ordered
pair. `"reference"` weights only the reference endpoint: it asks about structure
around salient reference edges, including nonsalient endpoints. Neither mode
filters a saliency-multiplied image.

## Compare the original map with alternatives

To understand a weighted result, keep the image fixed and change the map.
These alternative maps are **controls**: they help you ask what accounts for a
difference in entropy. Alongside the unweighted image, the function provides:

- **A centre map**, labelled `centre_bias`, which puts more weight near the
  middle of the image regardless of its content.
- **Flipped or rotated versions of the supplied map**, which preserve its
  weight values but move them relative to image features. The earlier
  `flip_axis1` comparison is one example.
- **Maps borrowed from other images**, when you supply them. The API calls
  each borrowed map a **donor map**. This lets you compare the image's own
  saliency map with maps associated with other images, without breaking those
  maps into randomly shuffled pixels.

Weighting changes the descriptor. It can increase or decrease entropy: a
concentrated map may emphasize regular structure, diverse structure, or weak
edges that counterbalance already uneven response strengths. The unweighted
contrast describes the **overall effect of weighting**. Exact map transforms
preserve the saliency value distribution and help examine alignment with this
particular image. Their overlap with image edges and their pair support can
still change.

Here, **alignment** means where the map's high weights fall relative to image
features. In our example, the bright spot's alignment with stripes rather than
noise explains why moving it changes first-order entropy.

The following values were supplied in the feature review. They are an
illustration for interpreting contrasts, not measurements from the synthetic
image above or a benchmark of the revised implementation.

```{r review-table, echo=FALSE}
review <- data.frame(control = c("unweighted", "centre_bias", "flip_axis1", "observed"),
  effective_fraction = c(1, .78, .34, .34),
  `20-80` = c(4.489, 4.459, 4.414, 4.292),
  `80-160` = c(4.443, 4.370, 4.262, 4.239),
  `160-240` = c(4.399, 4.375, 4.234, 4.247), check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(review, digits = 3, caption = "Illustrative review values; entropy in bits")
delta_unweighted <- unlist(review[4, 3:5] - review[1, 3:5])
delta_flipped <- unlist(review[4, 3:5] - review[3, 3:5])
knitr::kable(rbind(`Observed minus unweighted` = delta_unweighted,
                  `Observed minus flipped` = delta_flipped), digits = 3)
```

All three observed-minus-unweighted values are negative. Against the flipped
map, the additional reduction is mainly short-range; the long-range difference
is slightly positive. This one example does not establish a general effect.
Moreover, those raw summaries may average different combinations of distances
and directions. Each such combination is called a **cell**. A cell is left out
if it has too little weighted edge-pair support under the chosen validity rule.

To compare the same cells, we can restrict both maps' calculations to the cells
that are available for both. This is called **common support**. The output
includes this comparison alongside the original difference:

```{r common-support}
result$ranges[result$ranges$control == "flip_axis1",
  c("start", "end", "observed_minus_control", "observed_minus_control_common",
    "common_valid_cell_coverage", "common_status")]
```

`observed_minus_control_common` intersects the two maps' valid cells before
averaging. Both maps use equal weight for shared directions at each distance,
then equal weight for retained distances. `common_valid_cell_coverage` records
how much of the range survived this intersection.

The signs of first-order and pairwise contrasts differ in this constructed
example. These measures describe different distributions: marginal orientations
versus relative orientations conditional on distance and direction. There is no
requirement that weighting move them together.

The output also summarizes controls in two groups, called **families**: flipped
or rotated maps (`transformed`), and maps from other images (`donor`). Within
each group, it keeps cells available for the observed map and **all usable
distinct comparison maps**. This is more restrictive than comparing two maps
at a time. A transformation that leaves the map unchanged is excluded, and
repeated copies of the same map receive no extra votes. The mean and SD describe
the control values; the SD is not a standard error or a permutation-test
uncertainty estimate.

```{r family-summary}
result$comparisons[, c("family", "metric", "range_id", "observed_minus_control_mean",
                       "n_controls", "common_valid_cell_coverage", "status")]
```

The observed rows of `features` and `ranges` also contain
`observed_minus_transform_mean` and `observed_minus_donor_mean`. The pairwise
versions always use the family-wide common support. Other control rows have NA
in these columns. Because we have not yet supplied maps from other images,
that group's summary is unavailable. We add them in the next section.

The fixed `centre_bias` map uses `centre_sigma = .25`. With
`centre_match = TRUE`, a second map, `centre_bias_matched`, fits an isotropic
Gaussian in normalized image coordinates to the observed effective fraction.
Matching this one entropy value does not match shape, multimodality, edge overlap
or pair support. The fit can be unattainable on a discrete grid, for example a
one-pixel point mass versus a centred Gaussian on an even-by-even grid. Inspect
the fit status and achieved fraction rather than assuming success.

```{r centre-fit}
result$metadata$controls$centre_bias_matched
```

## Add comparison maps from other images

For a collection of images, you can ask whether each image's own saliency map
produces a different result from maps associated with the other images. First,
choose which images are suitable comparisons: they should have compatible
aspect ratios and maps produced by the same model and preprocessing steps.
`saliency_donor_assignments()` then chooses which other image's map to use for
each target image.

The `strata` argument expresses these matching groups: only images with the
same group label can exchange maps. This does not automatically match map
concentration. Add concentration to your grouping rule if your study requires
it, and inspect the effective fractions after any resizing. A borrowed map
retains its own pattern of weights, which may be more or less concentrated
than the target image's map.

Here we create synthetic stand-ins for two other images' maps. We label all
three images as belonging to the same matching group and request two sets of
assignments with `replicates = 2L`.

```{r donor-controls}
other_maps <- list(
  other_a = outer(1:72, 1:80, function(x, y) exp(-((x-55)^2+(y-30)^2)/180)),
  other_b = outer(1:72, 1:80, function(x, y) exp(-((x-40)^2+(y-65)^2)/350))
)
assignments <- saliency_donor_assignments(
  c("scene", "other_a", "other_b"), rep("same-grid-model-processing", 3),
  replicates = 2L, seed = 7L
)
with_other_maps <- do.call(compute_saliency_features, c(
  list(image = img, saliency = saliency, representation = "weights",
       image_id = "scene", donor_maps = other_maps, donor_assignments = assignments),
  settings))
with_other_maps$comparisons[with_other_maps$comparisons$family == "donor",
  c("metric", "range_id", "n_requested", "n_controls", "controls_used",
    "observed_minus_control_mean", "status")]
```

Assignments exclude the same stimulus, including alternate versions identified
with `stimulus_ids`. Random-number state is restored. Randomized matching does
not sample all admissible permutations uniformly, so these are descriptive
controls, not calibrated permutation p-values.

Keep these summaries separate from those for flipped or rotated maps. Combining
them into one mean would make the result depend on how many assignments from
other images you requested. The output reports `n_requested` and `n_controls`
separately because repeated assignments can reuse a map; each distinct map
receives one vote in the summary.

## Inspect support and resizing

```{r support}
result$ranges[result$ranges$control == "observed",
  c("start", "end", "entropy", "mass_fraction", "effective_pairs_ratio",
    "valid_cell_coverage", "status")]
```

`effective_pairs_ratio` compares Kish effective counts with the unweighted
counts on the **same selected edges**. A value of 0.22 describes a reduction in
weight spread relative to that baseline, not retention of 22% of independent
observations. Pairs share endpoints. Effective count is not an upper bound on
categorical entropy and is not an automatic bias correction.

Low `valid_cell_coverage` means the summary represents only part of its nominal
range. Inspect `result$cells$observed` to find which cells are missing or have
concentrated weights. Compact hotspots can leave long ranges unavailable even
when some positive mass reaches those distances. NA is distinct from a valid
entropy of zero. `validity = "support"` requires explicit
`min_cell_mass_fraction` and `min_effective_pairs`; these replace the legacy mass
cutoff. `min_common_coverage` can additionally reject comparisons with too little
shared coverage. Its default zero requires at least one shared cell and does
not certify adequate support for a scientific interpretation.

Both backends of this new API use Euclidean geometry and the native legacy
validity rule. The historical R conventions remain in
`compute_edge_entropy(use_cpp = FALSE)`. Uniform saliency retains native legacy
results; ordinary numerical tolerance applies to comparisons between backends.

Map downsampling uses area averaging, upsampling uses linear interpolation, and
mass is renormalized afterward. These operations can change concentration.
Metadata for the supplied map and maps from other images record location metrics
before and after resizing. For maps from other images, the default aspect-ratio
tolerance is 1%, intended for small grid-rounding differences, not for accepting
a different field of view. Keep smoothing and
viewing geometry consistent across images; record model and smoothing details
with `provenance`. No additional smoothing is applied here.

## Examine spatial organization at several scales

```{r multiscale}
curve <- result$multiscale$observed$summary
plot(curve$scale, curve$effective_fraction, type = "b", log = "x",
     xlab = "Block size / shorter image dimension",
     ylab = "Effective fraction", ylim = c(0, 1))
```

The curve aggregates probability into blocks at several shifted grid origins.
Boundary blocks use their actual areas in the uniform reference. Inspect
`result$multiscale$observed$curve` for individual origins. This is multiscale
location entropy, not second-order entropy; it describes clustering without
uniquely identifying the number or arrangement of hotspots. Use degrees of
visual angle with `scale_units = "degrees"` and `pixels_per_degree` when that
calibration is available. Arbitrary resampling and smoothing are not invariances.

## Plan runtime

The main example above took `r format(round(elapsed, 3), nsmall = 3)` seconds in
this build. It uses a 72-by-80 image and reduced filters and bins, so this is not
a prediction for full-size stimuli. Pairwise work grows quadratically with the
number of selected edges and roughly linearly with the number of controls after
sharing geometry. Default image selection shares one geometry pass and one
unweighted baseline across controls. Saliency-based selection may require
separate passes, and ties can increase the selected edge count above 10,000.

Use `pairwise = FALSE` for first-order and map descriptors alone. Benchmark a
representative image with `system.time()` before processing a corpus; record
image dimensions, selected edge counts, controls, bins and backend. The R
backend provides a slower reference implementation. Neither a smoke test nor
this small runnable example establishes production throughput.

```{r restore-rng, include=FALSE}
if (is.null(old_seed)) {
  if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE))
    rm(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv)
} else assign(".Random.seed", old_seed, envir = .GlobalEnv)
```
